name: EIA weekly crude inventory surprise trading

origin.source_title: The Effect of Oil Price Shocks on Asset Markets: Evidence from Oil Inventory News (Bank of Canada SWP 2020-8; Journal of Futures Markets 2020)

how_it_works.simple: Every Wednesday the US government says how much oil is in storage. If there is much less than people guessed, oil prices tend to jump up within minutes; if there is much more, they drop.
how_it_works.analogy: Like a shop announcing its stock count: if shelves are emptier than expected, buyers rush and prices rise.
how_it_works.precise: The surprise is the reported change in commercial crude, gasoline and distillate inventories minus the Bloomberg survey median, standardized. Crude futures move against the surprise inside a 15-minute window, and Alquist, Ellwanger and Jin use this as an instrument to show oil shocks move the US dollar and equities. A trading rule must act within seconds to minutes.

rule: At the Wednesday 10:30 ET Weekly Petroleum Status Report, compute surprise = actual crude inventory change minus consensus median; if the standardized surprise is below -1 go long front WTI futures, if above +1 go short; exit after 15 to 30 minutes. A slower variant trades oil-linked currencies (for example USD/CAD) in the same direction as the implied oil move.
data_needed: EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report history (free)
Consensus forecasts of inventory changes (Bloomberg or similar, paid)
Intraday WTI futures and FX prices
economic_rationale: Inventory surprises change the perceived supply and demand balance, so prices react (Alquist, Ellwanger and Jin 2020; Miao et al. 2017); higher oil prices from this news depreciate the US dollar against a broad range of currencies.
why_it_might_fail: The reaction is nearly instant, prices move in anticipation of the surprise (Miao et al. 2017), and the effect on crude roughly halved after 2008 in Alquist, Ellwanger and Jin's estimates; the edge needs paid consensus data and fast execution.

reported_results.source: Alquist, Ellwanger and Jin (2020), Bank of Canada SWP 2020-8, first-stage results
reported_results.market: WTI crude futures, 15-minute window around release
reported_results.notes: Event study, not a trading backtest. A one standard deviation positive crude inventory surprise lowered crude prices by about 0.57%; gasoline and distillate surprises by about 0.30% and 0.38%.

reported_results.source: Alquist, Ellwanger and Jin (2020), Bank of Canada SWP 2020-8, first-stage results
reported_results.market: WTI crude futures, 15-minute window around release
reported_results.notes: After 2008 the effect of a one standard deviation crude surprise fell to about 0.32%. The inventory news explains about 33% of oil price variation in the announcement window across the full sample.

reported_results.source: Miao, Ramchander, Wang and Yang (2017), Journal of Futures Markets abstract
reported_results.notes: Futures returns fall with positive surprises and rise with negative ones, with no asymmetry; prices move in anticipation. Abstract read via the OpenAlex record; no numbers given there.

post_publication_evidence: Alquist, Ellwanger and Jin report the price response to crude inventory news shrank after 2008 (about 0.57% to about 0.32% per standard deviation). No out-of-sample trading results were found.

relevance.reason: A clean, scheduled commodity news event that the paper links directly to US dollar moves, which fits parity's commodity and macro news angle.
